new_statements.quote: Stress phenomena have gone largely unmentioned in most descriptions of Bantoid languages (and Eastern Grassfields languages are no exception). This author feels that the reason for this is that amplitude phenomena in these languages are mostly predictable, perhaps to compensate for the complexity of its tonal phenomena [...] 6.1 Nouns and Verbs: First syllable of root. For nouns and verbs with single roots, it appears that the first syllable of the root is stressed. This means that all noun and verb prefixes and any second syllables on the roots are unstressed. [...] Grassfields Bantu languages, in general, are known for their tonal complexity.
new_statements.citation: Anderson, Stephen C. 2005. Phonological characteristics of Eastern Grassfields languages. In: Beban Sammy Chumbow, Ngessimo M. Mutaka et al. (eds.), Research Mate in African Linguistics: Focus on Cameroon. A fieldworker's tool for deciphering the stories Cameroonian languages have to tell, pp. 33-52 (approx.).
new_statements.locator: sec. 6 'Stress' and 6.1, sec. 7 'Tone' (printed pp. 47-48 of Research Mate; scanned text lines ~3374-3420 of the archive.org)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Work exists but A's citation needs correcting: Glottolog 5.3 ref 102337 = Anderson, Stephen Craig 2001, 'Phonological characteristics of Eastern Grassfields languages', in Mutaka & Chumbow (eds.), Research mate in African linguistics: focus on Cameroon (Grammatische Analysen afrikanischer Sprachen 17), Cologne: Ruediger Koeppe, pp. 33-54 (listed by Glottolog as a phonology, linked to no languoid); OpenLibrary OL18944990W gives 2001/Koeppe as well. So year is 2001 not 2005, pages 33-54, and in_glottolog should be 'yes' (as a reference, though not attached to kwaj1242 or Mfumteic). The archive.org item research-mate-cameroon itself could not be re-opened today (archive.org refused/timed out e…
new_statements.relation_note: Family-level: EGB languages are tonal (4 underlying noun melodies L-H, L-HL, L-LH, L-L in Ngiemboon; floating tones; downstep/register lowering); stress = predictable root-initial amplitude.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Eastern Grassfields languages generally (author's impression, exemplified by Ngiemboon): complex lexical/grammatical tone (four underlying noun melodies, floating tones, downstep); amplitude-stress predictable and non-contrastive, falling on the first syllable of the noun/verb root, with prefixes and root-second syllables unstressed; functors probably unstressed (unresearched).
new_statements.exceptions: functors may receive stress under contrastive focus (speculative, 'awaits future research'); author cautions that Ngiemboon is conservative and not all details will hold in related languages
new_statements.identity_note: FAMILY-LEVEL sketch of 'Eastern Grassfields' as delimited by Dieu & Renaud 1983, explicitly including the 'North (Limbum, Yamba, Mfumte, etc.)' subgroup to which Kwaja (ALCAM 905 Mfumte group) belongs; all examples are from Ngiemboon (Bamileke) and the author warns that not every detail holds across the family. It contains no Kwaja, Ndaktup or Mfumte data. It is therefore a secondhand/generalizing statement, not a first-hand description of kwaj1242.
